response.answer_text: DNA polymerase can only extend a new strand in the 5' to 3' direction, so new DNA is synthesized only in the 5' to 3' direction [ev_006]. At the replication fork, one template strand is oriented 3' to 5' and the other 5' to 3' [ev_001]. The new strand complementary to the 3' to 5' parental strand can be synthesized continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [ev_001]. The other new strand, complementary to the 5' to 3' parental strand, is extended away from the replication fork in small fragments called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The leading strand can be extended from a single primer, whereas the lagging strand needs a new primer for each short Okazaki fragment [ev_001]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [ev_002]. RNA primers are replaced by DNA as synthesis proceeds: DNA pol I removes the primers by its exonuclease activity, uses the DNA behind the RNA as its own primer, and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides [ev_002]. The remaining nicks between the newly synthesized DNA and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the adjacent fragment [ev_002].
